blocks.text: [II, 667] because Moses (Num. XI, 31.) and David (Psal. LXXVIII, 28.) write that they were not only carried by the south wind but also thrown down onto the ground. And indeed it is utterly false that they never fly with the south wind. For they are migratory birds: just as the north winds carry them away from us in autumn, so the south winds bring them back to us in spring. Aristotle, in the place cited above: Ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ οἱ ὄρτυγες (ἀπαίρουσι)· ἐὰν μή τινες ὑπολειφθῶσι ἐν εὐηλίοις χωρίοις· [Homoiōs de kai hoi ortyges (apairousi)· ean mē tines hypoleiphthōsi en euēliois chōriois·] Likewise the quails also (depart), unless a few have remained in sunny places. Varro, Rustic. book 3, ch. 5: Thrushes fly every year across the sea into Italy around the autumn equinox, and fly back to the same place at the spring equinox. And at another time turtledoves and quails, in enormous numbers. Pliny: Quails also always arrive before the cranes. Solinus: They have their times of arrival when summer has been driven off; or rather winter, as the great commentator on Solinus shows at length. Aloysius Mundella in his Letters: To the coastal region around Pesaro a huge number of quails usually arrives, and they are caught with a thousand snares; but their arrival has been observed chiefly toward the end of spring. Belon, Observat. book 2, ch. 17, on the voyage from Rhodes to Alexandria: Very many quails, flying from the north toward the south, were caught on our ship. From this I am firmly convinced that quails are migratory birds. For earlier, when I was sailing in spring from Zacynthus to Euboea, I had observed others flying in the opposite direction, from the south to the north. Gesner: Quails come to us, as I hear, at about the middle of April, and leave when the first frost sets in. From these it is clear not only that quails change their country, but also that in mid-spring they migrate from the south to the north. I note this here because at precisely that time the south wind brought quails into the camp of the Israelites, namely on the 24th day of the second month. For on the twentieth they had departed from the wilderness of Sinai; and after a three days' journey, when they had demanded meat with much murmuring, God promised that on the next day he would give it for a whole month, and he sent quails. See Num. X, 11. 12. 33. and XI, 18.

IV. As to the quantity, the Psalmist says that God rained quails like dust and like the sand of the sea, Psal. LXXVIII, 27, that is, sent them down in great quantity and abundance. Thus in Athenaeus, book 8, Phaenias relates ἐν Χεῤῥονήσῳ ἐπὶ τρισὶν ἡμέραις ὗσαι τὸν Θεὸν ἰχθύας [en Cherrhonēsō epi trisin hēmerais hysai ton Theon ichthyas], that in the Chersonese God rained fish for three days. And Phylarchus in the same place: ἑωρακέναι τινὰς πολλαχοῦ τὸν Θεὸν ὕσαντα ἰχθῦσιν, πολλάκις δὲ καὶ πυροῖς [heōrakenai tinas pollachou ton Theon hysanta ichthysin, pollakis de kai pyrois], that some have observed God raining fish in many places, and often wheat too. And Heraclides Lembus: Περὶ τὴν Παιονίαν [II, 668] καὶ Δαρδανίαν βατράχους, φησὶν, ὕσεν ὁ Θεὸς καὶ τοσοῦτον αὐτῶν ἐγένετο τὸ πλῆθος, ὡς τὰς οἰκίας καὶ τὰς ὁδοὺς πλήρεις εἶναι· [Peri tēn Paionian kai Dardanian batrachous, phēsin, hysen ho Theos kai tosouton autōn egeneto to plēthos, hōs tas oikias kai tas hodous plēreis einai·] Around Paeonia and Dardania, he says, God rained such a mass of frogs that they filled the houses and the roads. See the rest there, and the note on Exodi VIII, 3. In the same way God rained quails in such [col. 105] quantity that they were like dust,
— — — and of the sand that has no number.
